Alternative Solution 1:

We show that such coefficients can indeed be constructed.

Let us choose positive numbers
\[
a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_{19},
\]
all very close to one another. For concreteness, take
\[
a_i=M+i\varepsilon \qquad (i=0,1,\dots,19),
\]
where \(M>0\) is large and \(\varepsilon>0\) is very small.

Now consider the one-parameter family
\[
F_t(x)=x^{20}+a_{19}x^{19}+t\,x^{18}+a_{17}x^{17}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0,
\]
where \(t\) will vary. For very large \(t\), the coefficient of \(x^{18}\) is so large that \(F_t(x)>0\) for all real \(x\): this is obvious for \(x\ge 0\), and for \(x<0\) the term \(t x^{18}\) can be made to dominate the negative odd-power contributions on every bounded interval, while \(x^{20}\) dominates for \(|x|\) large.

On the other hand, when \(t=a_{18}\) and \(M\) is chosen large, we may evaluate at a fixed negative number, say \(x=-M\). Then
\[
F_{a_{18}}(-M)=(-M)^{20}+a_{19}(-M)^{19}+a_{18}(-M)^{18}+\cdots+a_0.
\]
Since \(a_{19}\approx M\), the term \(a_{19}(-M)^{19}\) is of size \(-M^{20}\), and by taking \(M\) large the odd term of degree \(19\) dominates the remaining terms in sign, so \(F_{a_{18}}(-M)<0\). Thus for \(t=a_{18}\), the polynomial has a negative value somewhere.

Hence there exists a smallest \(t_0>a_{18}\) such that
\[
F_{t_0}(x)\ge 0 \qquad \text{for all real }x.
\]
By minimality and continuity, \(F_{t_0}\) must have a real root \(r\). Since all coefficients are positive, \(F_{t_0}(x)>0\) for \(x\ge 0\), so necessarily \(r<0\).

We next show that in fact \(r<-1\). Indeed, if \(-1\le r<0\), then for each pair of consecutive exponents \((2k+1,2k)\),
\[
a_{2k+1}r^{2k+1}+t_0 r^{2k}
\]
or more generally
\[
a_{2k+1}r^{2k+1}+a_{2k}r^{2k}
= r^{2k}\bigl(a_{2k}+a_{2k+1}r\bigr)
\]
is nonnegative because \(a_{2k}>a_{2k+1}>0\) and \(r\in[-1,0)\), so \(a_{2k}+a_{2k+1}r\ge a_{2k}-a_{2k+1}>0\). Adding these nonnegative pair-contributions and also \(r^{20}>0\), we get \(F_{t_0}(r)>0\), contradiction. Therefore \(r<-1\).

Now fix this negative number \(r<-1\). Then the values
\[
r^{19},r^{17},\dots,r,\ 1,\ r^2,r^4,\dots,r^{18}
\]
are strictly increasing. Indeed, among the odd powers they are negative and become less negative as the exponent decreases, while all even powers are positive and increase with exponent for \(|r|>1\).

At the same time, the coefficients of \(F_{t_0}\) are arranged in exactly the same increasing order:
\[
a_{19}<a_{17}<\cdots<a_1<a_0<t_0<a_2<\cdots<a_{18},
\]
provided \(\varepsilon\) is small and \(t_0\) lies just above \(a_{18}\). Thus, by the rearrangement inequality, the sum
\[
r^{20}+c_{19}r^{19}+\cdots+c_0
\]
is strictly maximized when the coefficients \(c_i\) are matched to the powers in this order. Therefore, among all polynomials obtained by permuting the coefficients, the original \(F_{t_0}\) gives the largest value at \(x=r\). Since \(F_{t_0}(r)=0\), every nontrivial permutation \(Q\) satisfies
\[
Q(r)<0.
\]

Now increase \(t_0\) slightly to \(t_0+\delta\), with \(\delta>0\) very small, and define
\[
P(x)=x^{20}+a_{19}x^{19}+(t_0+\delta)x^{18}+a_{17}x^{17}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0.
\]
Because \(t_0\) was minimal, this small increase makes
\[
P(x)>0 \qquad \text{for all real }x,
\]
so \(P\) has no real root.

But for every polynomial obtained by swapping two coefficients, evaluate at the same point \(r\). Such a swapped polynomial differs from one of the nontrivial permutations above only by an arbitrarily small perturbation of the \(x^{18}\)-coefficient, so for sufficiently small \(\delta\) it still satisfies
\[
Q(r)<0.
\]
On the other hand, all these polynomials have positive leading term and even degree, hence
\[
Q(x)\to +\infty \qquad \text{as }x\to -\infty.
\]
Therefore each such \(Q\) has at least one real root.

Verification: the constructed \(P\) has all coefficients positive, satisfies \(P(x)>0\) for all real \(x\), and every polynomial formed by swapping any two coefficients is negative at \(x=r\) and positive for \(x\ll 0\), so each swapped polynomial has a real root.

Final Answer: \(\text{Yes}\)
